note: Holds industry context, judgment dimensions, extra questions, evidence interpretation and job links. Industries do not change scores: `axis_emphasis` marks the axes an industry looks at more closely, and it does not enter the axis level calculation. ME_V3_2 added three fields. `scene` is a short introduction shown before Core screening and produces no score. `judgement_dimensions` are the twelve judgments the industry actually requires of mechanical engineers, and the items take ten of them. `gap_language` and `result_line` are read when the report explains gaps in that industry's own terms.
reading_rule: An industry pack is not an industry trivia quiz. What it looks at is whether existing mechanical engineering experience can be recognized in, and connected to, that industry's problem situations. So for each item, `gloss` restates the judgment in general mechanical engineering terms, and the test screen shows that line together with the item. Not knowing industry jargon is never recorded as a poor fit: the report only goes as far as `in this industry, this is called...`. That is why items never ask whether you know a term, like `Have you managed particles?`, and instead say `Have you treated the ways contamination gets in as a design condition?`

exploration.note: All eight industries can be explored in the results. At the start of the assessment you pick up to two industries of interest, read the scenes for those industries before Core screening, and in PRO one of them is asked about in depth. Industries you did not pick are compared lightly through your Core results. The structure is not to be changed so that industry packs open only with a subscription.

demands: Holds position and shape accuracy at the nanometer-to-micron scale throughout the process
Equipment has to give the same values again and again even under vacuum, heat and vibration at the same time
Contamination shows up directly in yield, so materials, surfaces and airflow are considered together
Equipment downtime is written into the contract terms with the customer
packs.scene: In semiconductor equipment, mechanical engineers deal with problems such as precision structures, thermal deformation, vibration, vacuum and keeping equipment from stopping. Choosing materials, setting dimensions and confirming by measurement all carry over directly.

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you control thermal deformation at the design stage?
judgement_dimensions.why: Temperature differences between the chamber and the stage turn directly into position error

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you allocate accuracy among the parts?
judgement_dimensions.why: Overall accuracy is decided by where the tolerance budget is concentrated

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you turn vacuum and cleanroom conditions into material conditions?
judgement_dimensions.why: Materials that outgas cannot be used, and surface treatment becomes a condition

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you confirm vibration of moving axes by measurement?
judgement_dimensions.why: If vibration remains, alignment will be off

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you cut off the paths contamination takes through design?
judgement_dimensions.why: Contamination is not caught after it appears; you block the way it gets in

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you manage equipment downtime in numbers?
judgement_dimensions.why: Uptime is part of the delivery terms

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you check whether the same value comes out again?
judgement_dimensions.why: A value that matched once is not evidence

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you vary conditions to find the working range?
judgement_dimensions.why: The width of the process window is what produces yield

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you try different combinations of material and surface treatment?
judgement_dimensions.why: Even with the same geometry, the surface decides the result

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you capture repeated calculations and decisions so they can be reused?
judgement_dimensions.why: There are many equipment types, so the same calculations come up again and again

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you measure positioning accuracy repeatedly?
judgement_dimensions.why: The specification is repeatability, not one-time accuracy

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you narrow down causes so a failure does not happen again?
judgement_dimensions.why: If the same failure happens twice, it becomes a contract issue

items.ask: Have you set a shape and material with a special environment, such as vacuum or high temperature, as a condition?
items.gloss: Choosing the material and shape of a part used where temperature or pressure is out of the ordinary

items.ask: To meet overall accuracy, have you allocated tolerances among the parts?
items.gloss: Deciding which parts get tighter tolerances so the assembly meets its accuracy

items.ask: Have you calculated deformation caused by temperature differences in advance and revised a design?
items.gloss: Calculating how much a part grows when heated and changing dimensions or how it is fixed

items.ask: Have you treated the ways contamination gets in, or cleanliness, as a design condition?
items.gloss: Deciding covers or gap structures to keep dust or oil out

items.ask: Have you confirmed vibration or position error on a moving axis by measurement?
items.gloss: Measuring how much a moving part shakes and whether it stops where you want it to

items.ask: Have you measured several times under the same conditions to check that the value comes out again?
items.gloss: Measuring at several points to see whether values differ by location even within the same device

items.ask: Have you varied conditions to find the range that works?
items.gloss: Varying temperature, pressure or speed to find the range where things work well
items.review_reason: The judgment of finding a condition window is 0.59 similar to BATTERY_I3. The conditions that differ in semiconductors (yield and the process window) are missing from the wording.

items.ask: Have you recorded the time between failures to reduce equipment downtime?
items.gloss: Recording how many times and for how long lab equipment stopped

items.ask: When the same abnormality kept recurring, have you separated the equipment side from the process side?
items.gloss: When the same problem keeps happening, separating whether the equipment or the operating conditions are at fault

items.ask: Have you captured repeated calculations or decisions so others could use them?
items.gloss: Organizing frequent calculations into a table or procedure so others can use them too

demands: Requirements arrive as specification documents, and how each one will be verified is decided in advance
Weight has to come down while strength and life are maintained, so you need evidence to justify reducing safety margins
Shock, vibration and temperature ranges are wider than for ordinary products
Leaving a record of the basis for decisions is half of the deliverable
packs.scene: In defense and aerospace, mechanical engineers turn requirements that arrive as specifications into dimensions and materials, trade weight against strength, make things withstand wide temperature and vibration ranges, and leave a record of the basis for those judgments.

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you turn requirements in specification documents into design conditions?
judgement_dimensions.why: Requirements come as sentences, and design only starts once they are turned into conditions

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you decide what will count as meeting each requirement?
judgement_dimensions.why: The verification method is decided together with the requirement

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you build the case for trading weight against strength?
judgement_dimensions.why: Every decision to reduce weight demands a strength justification

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you decide where to put the safety factor?
judgement_dimensions.why: It has to be set between the value a standard gives and actual test values

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you treat a wide temperature range as a condition?
judgement_dimensions.why: The operating range is wider than for civilian products

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you anticipate shock and vibration testing at the design stage?

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you choose materials and processes within the specification?
judgement_dimensions.why: Usable materials are limited to an approved list

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you leave a traceable record of your reasoning?

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you list failure modes in advance?
judgement_dimensions.why: A single failure means mission failure

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you feed test results back into the design?
judgement_dimensions.why: A test is not a stamp of approval; it is design input

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you align the interfaces between several teams?
judgement_dimensions.why: One system is built in pieces by several organizations

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you manage schedule and changes through records?
judgement_dimensions.why: A single change can shift the certification schedule

items.ask: Have you broken requirements written as sentences into numerical conditions that can be met?
items.gloss: Turning the wording of competition rules or a project call into numerical conditions to meet

items.ask: Have you attached acceptance criteria to each requirement, defining what counts as meeting it?
items.gloss: Deciding for each requirement whether it will be confirmed by test or by calculation

items.ask: Have you built a calculated case that a part still holds up while cutting the safety factor?
items.gloss: Reducing thickness to make something lighter and confirming by calculation that it still holds up

items.ask: Have you chosen yourself whether to use a standard value or a test value?
items.gloss: Deciding whether to use material values from a handbook or values you measured yourself

items.ask: Have you treated a wide operating temperature range as a design condition?
items.gloss: Setting design conditions so a product survives both midwinter and midsummer temperatures

items.ask: Have you revised a design in advance, anticipating shock or vibration tests?
items.gloss: Reinforcing a design in advance with drop or shake tests in mind

items.ask: Have you listed failure modes in advance and worked through their effects?
items.gloss: Writing down where and how something could fail, and working through the ones with the biggest impact first

items.ask: Have you taken test results and gone back to revise the design?
items.gloss: Revising a design after it failed to meet the criteria in a test

items.ask: Have you decided what had to be matched between several teams or parts?
items.gloss: When work is split across teams, settling in advance the mating dimensions and connection methods

items.ask: Have you recorded the basis for a judgment so it could be traced back later?
items.gloss: Documenting why something was decided so it can be revisited later

demands: Cost, weight and performance are decided on the same table
Millions of vehicles have to come out at the same quality, so what the process can handle becomes a design condition
Noise and vibration are quality that customers feel immediately
Changing one part shifts the schedules of several teams at once
packs.scene: In the automotive industry, mechanical engineers set dimensions while weighing cost, weight and performance together, look at process conditions so millions of units come out the same, reduce noise and vibration, and confirm service life through testing.

judgement_dimensions.why: Cost comes in as a design condition

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you build what mass production can handle into the design?

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you build the case for reducing weight?
judgement_dimensions.why: Fuel economy and driving range depend on weight

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you separate the transfer paths of noise and vibration?
judgement_dimensions.why: If you cannot separate the causes, you cannot build a countermeasure

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you confirm service life with accelerated testing?
judgement_dimensions.why: The warranty period has to be backed by testing

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you decide where the heat goes?
judgement_dimensions.why: With electrification, thermal design decides performance

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you narrow down the causes of field failures?
judgement_dimensions.why: Recall costs are bigger than design costs

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you calculate tolerance stack-up to confirm assembly?

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you trace the scope of impact of a change?
judgement_dimensions.why: A single part involves several teams

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you pick out the characteristics to control and set criteria?
judgement_dimensions.why: You cannot control everything

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you correlate testing with analysis?
judgement_dimensions.why: Analysis has to match testing to be used for the next model

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you revise shapes based on assembly and machining hours?
judgement_dimensions.why: Labor hours go straight into cost

items.ask: Have you revised a shape or material after looking at cost or machining hours?
items.gloss: Changing a shape or material to make something cheaper or faster to produce

items.ask: Have you built the range that can be mass-produced into the design conditions?
items.gloss: Revising a design after checking whether it could easily be made in quantity

items.ask: Have you looked for a way to reduce weight without raising cost?
items.gloss: Finding ways to reduce weight without increasing cost

items.ask: Have you separated where noise or vibration travels?
items.gloss: Measuring where noise or vibration comes from and where it travels

items.ask: Have you confirmed service life in a shortened, accelerated way to back a warranty period?

items.ask: Have you calculated in advance the dimensional variation that comes with producing in high volume?

items.ask: Have you picked out the characteristics to control and set criteria for them?

demands: What moves is the product, so weight, inertia and the power transmission method decide performance
Cycle time per operation and repeatability are the specifications, and the two pull against each other

packs.scene: In robotics and automation, mechanical engineers look at the weight and inertia of what has to move to choose motors and gearboxes, set the drivetrain and stiffness, balance cycle time against repeatability, and make machines safe to work alongside people.

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you choose the drive after working through load and inertia?
judgement_dimensions.why: If the selection is wrong, all the tuning that follows is wasted

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you trade cycle time against accuracy?
judgement_dimensions.why: Going faster costs accuracy

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you look at drivetrain stiffness and backlash?
judgement_dimensions.why: Some problems live in the mechanics and cannot be covered up by control

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you measure repeat positioning accuracy many times?
judgement_dimensions.why: Accuracy measured once is not a specification

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you separate the cause of vibration into stiffness versus gain?
judgement_dimensions.why: If you cannot separate the causes, you only shuffle the problem around

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you turn safety requirements into design conditions?
judgement_dimensions.why: It moves in the same space as people

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you separate manual work from what the device will do?
judgement_dimensions.why: Automating everything does not pay off

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you adjust specifications to site conditions?
judgement_dimensions.why: Every site has different space and different objects to handle

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you keep commissioning records?
judgement_dimensions.why: The next unit is built from those records

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you narrow down why the equipment stopped?
judgement_dimensions.why: When the line stops, losses start immediately

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you hand over operation and recovery to the users?
judgement_dimensions.why: If you cannot hand it over, the person who built it has to stay attached to it

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you capture repeated sizing calculations and reuse them?
judgement_dimensions.why: The same calculation is done for every unit

items.ask: Have you sized a motor after working through the weight and inertia of what had to move?

items.ask: Have you set the gear ratio or transmission type to meet the required accuracy?

items.ask: Have you written down separately which motions a person would do and which the device would do?

items.gloss: Writing down the order in which a device moves and the results of its trial runs

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you collect data in a usable form?
